f: make into a hollow shape
make soft and fluffy
make a loud boasting claim
r: be- + cloud
s: It was past four o’clock, and the beclouded afternoon was tending to drear twilight.

f: a servant who carries a palanquin in a procession
a dancer who performs at temple festivals in India
a clerk who keeps accounts for a tea merchant
r: Hindustani ḍakait, from ḍākā “gang-robbery”
s: On the way back Boyles led him down a lampless lane, and sure enough, a pair of dacoits pounced on them.

f: pale and sickly green
small and stooped
shy and peeping
r: Late Middle English pevish “capricious, wilful; perverse”; further origin uncertain
s: I would rather figure things out on my own than ask that peevish librarian for help.

f: clothing that is informal or relaxed and intended to be worn at home
cooking that is slow or simple and intended to use leftover meat in a stew
training that is harsh or repetitive and intended to toughen young soldiers
r: casuist + -ry
s: She meant to extract casuistry’s penalty in advance.

f: sort into; arrange by order of status
wrinkle up; fold into small creases
sprinkle over; scatter in small drops
r: Old French rancler “to ulcerate”, from Latin dracunculus “little serpent”
s: My colleague's gratuitous criticism still rankles with me.

f: rub (until sore, as with a rough collar, etc.)
separate (husks from grain, by tossing in the wind, etc.)
sing (in a soft voice, as birds at dusk, etc.)
r: Middle English chaffare “a bargain, a trade”: cheap + fare
s: To chaffer for preferment with his gold.

f: use of a phrase that contradicts itself though meant to be taken seriously
use of an ordinary word in place of a rude one to soften its effect
use of a long and complex sentence where a short one would serve
r: Greek zeûgma “yoking; a bond”, from zeúgnumi “to yoke; to join”
s: ‘Mr. Pickwick took his hat and his leave’ is an example of zeugma.

f: wide awake and alert
filled with wonder
watchful and suspicious
r: a- + weary
s: "Nay, save that she seems aweary".

f: a green color
a strong vinegar
a legal verdict
r: French verbiage; compare verb in its sense “word”
s: We're done drafting our paper except for the final check to see whether any verbiage can be reduced.

f: city planning; layout of streets
steady growth; rising numbers
formal dress; a top hat
r: Latin urbānitās, from urbānus “belonging to a city”, from urbs “city”
s: Wealdon's two little visits explained perfectly the active urbanities of Captain Stanley Lake.

f: a morbid fear of three-legged creatures
a morbid fear of walking under ladders
a morbid fear of mirrors and reflections
r: triskaideka- “thirteen” + -phobia
s: Paraskevidekatriaphobia — a specialized form of triskaidekaphobia.

f: relating to public baths
deep and dark
easily bruised
r: bathos + -etic, modeled on pathos and pathetic
s: The fall is indeed the archetypal bathetic motion.

f: soaked through
merry and festive
lazy on weekends
r: Middle English saturnine “under the influence of the planet Saturn”
s: The monstrous thought came into my mind as I perused the fixed eyes and the saturnine face, that this was a spirit, not a man.

f: absent from one’s post; failing to appear for duty without any good excuse
harsh and grating; producing a rough sound that is unpleasant to the ear
sudden and unexpected; happening without warning or any sign beforehand
r: Latin abstrūsus “concealed, hidden”, from abstrūdō “to conceal; to thrust away”
s: Made the most abstruse inquiries clear and facile to my apprehension.

f: the upper deck of a ship or aircraft where the crew sleeps when not on duty during long voyages
the wooden ramp of a ship or barge that is lowered onto the dock for loading horses and carts
the rear part of a ship or aircraft where the stores and spare equipment are kept below deck
r: Middle English ladde-bord, changed to larboard in the 1500s by association with starboard
s: "It means to turn to larboard."

f: excessively friendly; eager to make acquaintances with strangers
extremely thin; pale and weak from lack of food
strongly perfumed; smelling of flowers and spices
r: Old French frenetike, from Greek phrenētikós “delirious”
s: After a week of working at a frenetic pace, she was ready for Saturday.

f: happening once a year
cancelled by law
marked with fine lines
r: Latin ānulāris “ring-shaped”, from ānulus “ring”
s: Reminding them that the annular wing is a very old aeronautical principle.

f: free of bacteria
coarse and rustic
of Teutonic descent
r: A variant of german “having the same parents; related”
s: Yet this much is germane to the present inquiry.

f: a small bird that chirps at dusk
a stout walking stick of olive wood
a sweet liqueur flavored with cherries
r: Italian cicerone, after Cicero, the Roman orator
s: Ultimately their gazes all rested on his cicerone as most powerful member of the group.

f: having a poor or faulty shape
relating to men and boys
lacking enough to eat
r: Latin maleficus
s: I would have liked to know whether he thought this was due to the climate, the diet, or simply malefic djinns.

f: a boy who sings in a cathedral choir
a woman who keeps a small inn
a man who herds goats in the hills
r: Probably Middle Dutch heyden “heathen”
s: A great, strong, heavy girl, a hoyden, not pretty, her face distinguished only by youth, by health.

f: someone skilled in the handling of horses (especially racehorses)
someone devoted to the study of ancient languages (especially Latin)
someone employed in the making of gloves (especially in Italy)
r: Latin āmanuēnsis “secretary”, from ab- “from” + manus “hand”
s: I, his mere amanuensis, am left to do what little I can to keep the institution functioning.

f: a stiff wide petticoat
a loud wheezing cough
a child’s spinning top
r: Probably French houp-là “upsy-daisy”; first attested c. 1877
s: Campers enjoyed all of the traditional camp hoopla.

f: a garden enclosure
a city guard
a war cry
r: Old French guerdon, from Medieval Latin widerdōnum, literally ‘back-payment’
s: Verse, like the laurel its immortal meed, Should be the guerdon of a noble deed.

f: gain possession of
fall silent and still
clear of all blame
r: Latin acquiescō, from ad + quiescō “to rest”
s: They were compelled to acquiesce in a government which they did not regard as just.

f: someone or something that is regarded as a bad omen
someone or something that has been cast out of a group
someone or something that moves with silent stealth at night
r: Late Latin behemoth, from Hebrew behemót, likely an intensive plural of behemá “beast”
s: The conduits and pipes like the circulatory system of some vast planetary behemoth.

f: immoderately fond of keeping birds
varied in form or kind
eager to fly or travel by air
r: Latin avaritia “greed”, from avarus “greedy”
s: He was called a hard, avaricious, rapacious man, whose chief business was to enrich himself.

f: a stringed instrument played by wandering folk musicians
a colored scarf tied around the head by sailors
a thin strip of cloth wrapped around a wound
r: Middle French bandoulliere, from Catalan bandolera, from bàndol “band, faction”
s: We had each bandoliers of cartridges.

f: having half the usual number of musical notes
having the shape of a half circle or arch
happening twice in every month of the year
r: Latin sempiternus, from semper “always” + æternus “eternal”
s: Why not sempiternal Thou and I?

f: lightly salted (especially of fish)
narrowly pleated (especially of skirts)
thinly sliced (especially of bread)
r: Probably skite “to move lightly and hurriedly” + -ish
s: The dog likes people he knows, but he is skittish around strangers.

f: a state or condition of deep unconsciousness caused by illness or injury
a group or body of people chosen to manage a specific task
a situation or play that is lighthearted and meant to amuse an audience
r: Latin cōmitās
s: Comity and conciliation are a slog.

f: stroke a pet gently
fill with thick mist
fuss over small children
r: Back-formation from pettifogger
s: Don't pettifog or we will soon grow weary.
